name: Cree, Plains
confidence_why: No usable statement on word stress located.
sweep_summary: Plains Cree is in the catalog as 'excluded' (reason sources-undetermined: secondary-stress direction fork between Wolfart 1996:431 'either direction' and Okimasis & Ratt 1999 leftward; our check of 9/16 already holds Athanasopoulou et al. 2025 JIPA, Muehlbauer 2006, Cook 1991 and Wolfart 1973). Two works with stress in the title. (1) Wolfart 1989 'Prosodische Grenzsignale im Plains Cree' (Folia Linguistica 23:327-334) is closed (Unpaywall/Crossref/De Gruyter bot wall/HathiTrust search-only/no repository copy); I read three of its six citing works (Russell 1998 ZASPiL, Russell 2006/2008 sandhi draft, Shwayder 2015 diss., all downloaded to plus the held Wolvengrey 2011: all cite it only for word-boundary vowel sandhi/devoicing (kâ+i -> kê in realis clauses, sandhi in casual speech), none for stress placement, so relevance is unclear (boundary prosody, possibly including antepenult stress as a boundary signal); priority medium because a first-hand Wolfart statement from 1989 could bear on the 1996 direction fork. (2) Cook 1991 (Glottolog wrongly credits editor Cowan) was held by the project and re-read: antepenultimate primary accent, postlexical, with penult alternants from post-stress vowel/glide deletion; silent on secondary stress, so it refines but cannot close the fork; it is the best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title and does not supersede the catalog's deciding sources. Two side findings for the parent: (a) the archive.org 'rosettaproject_crk_detail-1' item marked OPEN ONLINE for Wolfart 1996 in is a one-page excerpt (p. 390, Introduction) and does not contain p. 431 (saved, checked); (b) the held Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 OSF draft (litreview/sources) reproduces Wolfart 1996:431's examples with feet marked ('adapted to the IPA and feet have been indicated', fn. 8): nêhiyaw /(ˈneː)(hiˌjaw)/ and pasakwâpisimowin /(ˌpa)(saˌkwaː)(piˈsi)(moˌwin)/, i.e. they read Wolfart's secondaries as bidirectional with a final secondary in trisyllables, which is exactly the reading the exclusion note calls unresolvable from scanned; second-hand, but worth logging against the fork. written in the save directory;org/HathiTrust/Penn DSpace/ZASPiL/UManitoba APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: The word stress or accent in Cree is largely predicted by a postlexical antepenultimate stress rule where rules of lexical derivation are organized in two or three strata. [...] Needless to say, there is a lot more to be learned of Cree stress or accent, but the analysis presented in this paper demonstrates the regularity of an antipenultimate stress where apparent counterexamples are accounted for in level ordered lexical derivation. Another point to be emphasized here is that "stress" is clearly an inadequate term as indicated by the stability phenomenon. I suggest that "accent" is a more appropriate term to use until more is known about the rhythmic pattern of Cree.
new_statements.citation: Cook, Eung-Do. 1991. Lexical derivation and stress in Cree. In William Cowan (ed.), Papers of the Twenty-Second Algonquian Conference, 21-29. Ottawa: Carleton University.
new_statements.reading: Fixed antepenultimate primary stress (better: accent) in polysyllabic nouns and verbs, assigned postlexically before optional vowel/glide deletions that create surface penult alternants; no statement on secondary stress, its direction, or disyllables; based on two speakers' citation forms.

Another point to be emphasized here is that…

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Cook 1991 (PAC 22: 21-29) is a first-hand (two northern-Alberta Plains Cree speakers, citation forms) statement of PRIMARY stress only: antepenultimate in polysyllabic nouns and verbs, assigned postlexically, with surface penult/antepenult alternants explained by later i-deletion, glide deletion and stress relinking (rules (8) p. 24, (14) p. 27). (Algonquian Papers - Archive vol. 37, ISSN 0831-5671; open PDF at ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/view/1145)
tone_statements.quote: In the nominal data under consideration, prominence is consistently realized by a falling pitch (the phonological correlate of fundamental frequency) on the penultimate syllable. ... Thus, Plains Cree exhibits a trochaic system in its nominal accentuation; the left syllable of a foot receives a pitch "accent." ... In the typology of prominence systems, this means that Plains Cree is not a prototypical case of any of the categories used by linguists ("stress," "pitch accent," or "tone").
tone_statements.summary: F0 study of 267 noun tokens: one rise-fall per prosodic word; the penult fall is the accent, the rise secondary; no tone inventory; author declines the labels stress/pitch accent/tone. 60+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Schmirler, Katherine & Anja Arnhold. 2025. A Typological Outlier Explained: Stress and Phrase-Level Prosody in Plains Cree. International Journal of American Linguistics 91(1): 97-147. doi:10.1086/732878
tone_statements.quote: Here, we show evidence of consistent prosodic patterns in both single-word and multi-word utterances, but argue that these patterns neither support ultimate, penultimate, nor antepenultimate stress. We suggest that prosodic patterns are best accounted for as marking the boundaries of prosodic domains, without reference to stress. [sec. 1, MS p. 2] ... the present study has taken a different approach and suggested that Plains Cree is not a stress-accent language. Instead, we propose that the regular pitch contours visible on Plains Cree words are realizations of tonal targets associated with a prosodic level above the level of the word, the phonological phrase. These tonal targets have tentatively been identified as a high tone associated with the beginning of the phrase and four tones realized as a rise-fall-rise associated with its end, i.e., H-LHLH. ... we suggest that words in Plains Cree do not bear any lexical prosodic information as expected in a stress, pitch-accent or tone language. [sec. 9, MS p. 49]

tone_statements.summary: Pitch, duration and intensity each show regular patterns (rising f0 on the antepenult and the final syllable, falling f0 on the penult, longer and quieter final syllables) but never converge on one syllable, so the authors reject antepenultimate, penultimate and ultimate stress and analyse Plains Cree as a phrase language with no word stress and no lexical tone or pitch accent: the pitch contours

Rewrite the exclusion reason from 'stress not determinable from the sources' to: 'word-stress status rejected/contested by instrumental work — Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 (IJAL 91:97-147): no word stress, phrase language (H.. LHLH phrasal tones); Athanasopoulou, Goddard & Flynn 2025 (JIPA 55:92-133, pp. 92, 128-129): predictable penult HL word-level pitch accent, not stress, duration not a cue; Muehlbauer 2006 (PAC 37:229-268): penult pitch fall; all three reject the antepenult-primary + alternating-secondary profile StressTyp2 codes from Wolfart 1996:431 / Okimasis & Ratt 1999:3-4, whose own statements disagree on secondary direction and which Wolfart 1973 fn. 58 called highly tentative.' Add these to refs/sources with the page locators above; the StressTyp2 contradiction note stands and is strengthened.
audit.deciding_source_year: 1996 (Wolfart HNAI sketch) vs 1999/2018 (Okimasis & Ratt pedagogical grammar) vs 1973 (Wolfart grammar); backed since 2026-08-18 by Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 (instrumental)
audit.reasoning: Record: classification excluded, no quote, reason 'not determinable from the sources' after the rejudge (Wolfart 1996:431 'either direction' vs Okimasis & Ratt 1999:3-4 leftward-only; Wolfart 1973 states no rule). I confirmed the Okimasis passage verbatim in the held 2018 open edition (pp. 6-7), the Wolfart 1973 hedges verbatim in the archive.org text downloaded now, and the Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 conclusion in the held OSF draft; the HNAI 17:431 page itself is not yet obtained (no open copy) but is corroborated via StressTyp2's passage bank and an independent page-cited quotation. Web search turned up a second 2025 instrumental study we did not have — Athanasopoulou, Goddard & Flynn, JIPA 55 (open access, downloaded, read pp. 92, 128-130): it too rejects antepenult stress and alternating rhythm, but unlike Schmirler & Arnhold it posits a predictable word-level penult HL pitch accent and says the languag

sources.citation: Muehlbauer, Jeff. 2006. Pitch as accent in Plains Cree nominals. In H.C. Wolfart (ed.), Actes du 37e Congres des Algonquinistes, 229-268. Winnipeg: University of Manitoba.
sources.quote: Conclusion: 'the penultimate syllable of a "word" will consistently have a low or dropping pitch... Plains Cree uses a falling fundamental frequency to express phonological prominences. In the typology of prominence systems, this means that Plains Cree is not a prototypical case of any of the categories used by linguists ("stress," "pitch accent," or "tone").' p. 260: 'the pitch prominence is usually two syllables from an edge, which implicates a bisyllabic, trochaic foot'. Acoustic (F0) study of spontaneous speech; no alternating secondary stresses reported.
sources.locator: pp. 229-230 (three prior accounts: Bloomfield 1930 antepenult, Edwards 1954 penult, Lacombe 1874 ultima); pp. 259-260; Conclusion p. 261
sources.note: The first acoustic account (penult pitch fall, trochaic foot at right edge); the 'penult' arm of the three-way split both 2025 studies build on.
sources.venue: Actes du 37e Congres des Algonquinistes

sources.note: Lacombe's 'accent' means vowel length (long vs short a, i), not stress; the grammar has no word-stress or prominence statement, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's antepenultimate reading (Cook 1991). tone.quote: 3.1 Stress is presumably non-phonemic.⁴ ... 4. Bloomfield's statement concerning the occurrence of stress is rather over-simplified ... Actually a high pitch (part of the unanalyzed intonational system) occurs a good deal more regularly on the antepenultimate syllable than the stress itself which may occur on either the antepenultimate or penultimate syllables. ... 5. Although the stress seems to fall regularly on the last syllable of disyllabic words, the pitch of the last syllable may be either lower or higher than that of the first syllable. With intonational pattern low-high, the utterance seems to be more emphatic; while with intonational pattern high-low it is more casual

tone.quote: A non-significant stress accent falls on the third syllable from the end of words or close-knit phrases: nä'hiyaw : a Cree; nähi'yawak : Crees; iskwä'w ana : that woman. Initial vowels have an on-glide of h under stress, especially in interjections; hay hay ! splendid! [...] [p. 3:] The stress, it will be noticed, of an elided short vowel, stays on the vowel with which it has merged. [...] [p. 4:] The sound s varies freely between normal and abnormal sibilant. It is often spoken long, especially after stressed vowels (i.e., after the antepenultimate vowel), e.g. in asiniy : stone, asamaw : he gives him to eat, misiwah : all over.
